algorithm.name: Bubble Sort
algorithm.introduction: A simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list...
algorithm.intuition: Imagine bubbles rising to the surface. The largest elements "bubble up" to the end of the array.

algorithm.name: Binary Search
algorithm.introduction: A search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array.
algorithm.intuition: Like searching a dictionary. Open to the middle, decide left or right, and repeat.
algorithm.interviewNotes: Fundamental. You must be able to write this bug-free in 2 minutes.

question.title: Binary Search
question.statement: Given an array of integers nums which is sorted in ascending order, and an integer target, write a function to search target in nums.
question.hints: ["Check the middle element", "Adjust left and right bounds"]

question.title: Two Sum II
question.statement: Given a 1-indexed array of integers sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific target.
question.hints: ["Use two pointers at opposite ends", "Move pointers based on sum"]

interviewMessage.content:
Hello! Welcome to your technical interview for the SDE 1 position. We'll be focusing today on Arrays, Trees. Let's begin with our first question:

Explain the difference between Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) in a binary tree. When would you prefer BFS over DFS?

BFS explores node level by level using a queue data structure, while DFS explores branch by branch using recursion or a stack. I would prefer BFS when finding the shortest path in an unweighted tree or graph, or when the target is likely close to the root. The time complexity for both is O(V + E) or O(N) for binary trees, and space complexity for BFS is O(W) where W is the maximum width of the tree.

Great point. Following up on that:

If a tree has depth 10,000 but only a few nodes per level, what is the risk of recursive DFS and how would you safeguard against it?

Hello! Welcome to your technical interview for the Full Stack Engineer position. We'll be focusing today on System Design, Arrays. Let's begin with our first question:

How does the React Reconciliation algorithm and Virtual DOM work? How does React optimize re-renders when rendering large dynamic lists?

To design a URL shortener, I would use Base62 encoding (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) to convert a 64-bit auto-incrementing ID or distributed Snowflake ID into a 7-character hash, allowing 3.5 trillion unique URLs. For high read throughput, I would place a distributed Redis cache layer in front of a relational or NoSQL database. Reads would issue HTTP 302 redirects to preserve analytics. Time complexity for lookup is O(1) in cache.

Great point. Following up on that:

Why is using array index as a key considered an anti-pattern when list items can be reordered or filtered?

Hello! Welcome to your technical interview for the Software Development Engineer position at difficulty Medium. Today we will focus on Data Structures and Algorithms, Object-Oriented Programming, DBMS and SQL.

Let's start with our first question:

Explain the Dynamic Programming approach to solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem versus the Fractional Knapsack problem. What makes one solvable with a greedy approach while the other requires DP?

" The fundamental difference lies in whether items can be divided. In Fractional Knapsack, items can be broken into smaller portions, so selecting items in descending order of their value-to-weight ratio always gives an optimal solution. Hence, a Greedy approach works.

However, in 0/1 Knapsack, items cannot be divided. Selecting the item with the highest value-to-weight ratio might prevent us from choosing a better combination of other items. Therefore, we use Dynamic Programming to consider both possibilities of including and excluding each item and obtain the globally optimal solution."

Good. Following up on your explanation:

What edge cases should you consider regarding duplicate elements or using the same element twice?

interviewEvaluation.questionText:
Hello! Welcome to your technical interview for the Software Development Engineer position at difficulty Medium. Today we will focus on Data Structures and Algorithms, Object-Oriented Programming, DBMS and SQL.

Let's start with our first question:

Explain the Dynamic Programming approach to solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem versus the Fractional Knapsack problem. What makes one solvable with a greedy approach while the other requires DP?
interviewEvaluation.candidateAnswer:
" The fundamental difference lies in whether items can be divided. In Fractional Knapsack, items can be broken into smaller portions, so selecting items in descending order of their value-to-weight ratio always gives an optimal solution. Hence, a Greedy approach works.

However, in 0/1 Knapsack, items cannot be divided. Selecting the item with the highest value-to-weight ratio might prevent us from choosing a better combination of other items. Therefore, we use Dynamic Programming to consider both possibilities of including and excluding each item and obtain the globally optimal solution."
interviewEvaluation.rationale: Clear explanation touching on the core principles.
